prompt: What does a case tool add that a folder of case documents does not?
hint: Think about what happens each time a case is executed.

choices.text: A safe, searchable place where a case is never lost or overwritten
choices.why: Storage is the smallest part of the job; a shared folder already keeps files.

choices.text: Each case kept apart from its runs, with one result per run
choices.why: Right: the case is written once and every execution records its own result against it.

choices.text: Steps written from the requirement for you
choices.why: The tool records cases a person writes; writing them well is lesson 3.

choices.text: A choice, made for you, of which cases to run in each release
choices.why: Choosing is the risk ranking and the regression decisions, made by people.

prompt: Booking answers every request with an error page, so the member discount case never reaches a price. What result does that case get?
hint: Did the discount get tested?

choices.text: Failed, since the expected price never appeared
choices.why: That says the discount is wrong, which nobody knows: the case never got that far.

choices.text: Blocked
choices.why: Right: it could not run because something it needs is broken, and the result points at that defect.

choices.text: Not run, with nothing more said
choices.why: Not run says nobody tried; somebody did try and was stopped, which is worth recording.

choices.text: Taken out of the run until booking works
choices.why: Then the run no longer shows that the discount went untested on this build.

prompt: TC-10 passed on 1.0 and failed on 1.1. What does a tool's results history show that two separate run documents do not?
hint: One row, two results.

choices.text: That TC-10 needs rewriting, because its result changed
choices.why: A changed result is evidence about the product, not about the case text.

choices.text: Nothing; the two documents hold the same two facts
choices.why: They hold the facts apart, and the connection between them is the finding.

choices.text: A regression: the result changed between releases
choices.why: Right: seen as one row, pass then fail is something 1.1 broke.

choices.text: That the 1.0 run was done less carefully than the 1.1 run
choices.why: Nothing in two results says how carefully either was run.

prompt: Rui asks what the student discount defect threatens. Put the links in the order the tool walks them, starting from the report.
hint: The figure in section 01, read from right to left.
items: The failed result in the 1.1 run
trap: Starting from the requirement is the other direction, the question "is R5 tested?".

prompt: Which of these is a reason for a team to move its cases into a case tool?
hint: Section 01 lists four situations.

choices.text: The cases say "check booking works" and nobody else can run them
choices.why: A tool stores vague cases exactly as vague; rewriting them is lesson 3.

choices.text: One tester looks after seventeen cases and one product
choices.why: That is the situation the spreadsheet of section 04 serves well.

choices.text: Nobody has decided which risks to test first
choices.why: That is a decision for the plan of lesson 1; no tool makes it.

choices.text: Three testers record results in the same run
choices.why: Right: several people writing one run at once is what a shared file handles worst.

prompt: Match each thing that happened to the result it gets.
hint: Four statuses mean the same thing in every tool.

pairs.left: Booking crashed, so the discount case never reached a price
Six tickets refused with "You can book 1 to 6 tickets."
Nobody has reached the case yet in this run
Order 1001 reserved, as the case expects

prompt: What kind of tool are TestRail and qTest?
hint: Where do they sit relative to the tracker?

choices.text: Defect trackers with a tab for test cases
choices.why: Defects stay in the tracker of lesson 17; these link to it.

choices.text: Case managers that sit beside a tracker
choices.why: Right: their whole subject is cases, runs and results, linked to the tracker.

choices.text: Apps installed inside Jira
choices.why: That describes Zephyr, the one that lives in the tracker.

choices.text: Open-source servers each team installs for itself
choices.why: That is TestLink; these two are sold by subscription.

prompt: In TestRail, Ana wants 1.1's regression cases run on four browsers. What shape does that take?
hint: Lesson 7's matrix, inside a tool.

choices.text: Four copies of the suite, one per browser
choices.why: Copies split one case into four, and its history with it.

choices.text: One run in which every case gets four results, one per browser
choices.why: A run holds one result per case; the browsers are separate runs.

choices.text: A test plan holding one test run per browser
choices.why: Right: the plan groups the runs that belong to one release.

choices.text: Four milestones
choices.why: A milestone ties work to a release date, not to a configuration.

prompt: Half of boxoffice's regression suite is automated. Why does it matter that the case tool has an API?
hint: How many answers to "did 1.1 pass?" does the team want?

choices.text: Automated results land in the same runs as manual ones
choices.why: Right: one run, one answer, whichever way each case was executed.

choices.text: It writes the automated tests from the manual cases
choices.why: It receives results; the tests are written by people, in the automation courses.

choices.text: So that manual cases are dropped
choices.why: Nothing about an API removes a case; that is a decision about the suite.

choices.text: So the automated tests run faster
choices.why: Speed belongs to the tests and the machine, not to where results are stored.

prompt: A manager asks every week which requirements have cases and which of those failed this cycle. In qTest, why is that cheap to answer?
hint: Where are the requirements kept?

choices.text: It marks a requirement passed once its cases exist
choices.why: Written is not run; coverage needs results from a cycle.

choices.text: The requirements are in the tool, so coverage is a view
choices.why: Right: the links already exist, so nobody assembles the report by hand.

choices.text: Because qTest keeps one requirement per test cycle
choices.why: Cycles hold runs of many cases citing many requirements.

choices.text: It copies the failures into Jira as stories
choices.why: Failures become defects, and the view is in qTest itself.

prompt: TestLink costs no licence. What does it cost instead?
hint: Who answers when it is down?

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: A server has to be installed, updated, backed up and watched by somebody.

choices.text: A fee per case once the repository passes a size
choices.why: Open source has no fee per case; the cost is in running it.

choices.text: Somebody's time to install it, update it, back it up and keep it running
choices.why: Right: and in a small company that somebody is often the tester.

choices.text: A Jira subscription, which it needs to run
choices.why: TestLink is its own web application with its own database.

prompt: A team uses one of Zephyr's Jira apps. Where do its cases and executions live?
hint: One place or two?

choices.text: In a separate Zephyr site beside Jira
choices.why: That is the standalone shape of TestRail and qTest.

choices.text: In the Jira project, with the stories and the defects
choices.why: Right: a failed execution and its bug are linked inside one tool.

choices.text: In a spreadsheet attached to each story
choices.why: Attachments are files, not runs with results.

choices.text: On the company's own server, like TestLink
choices.why: Zephyr goes wherever the company's Jira goes.

prompt: Match each tool to what it calls a run.
hint: The table at the end of section 03.

pairs.right: A test run, grouped in a test plan
A test run inside a test cycle
A test plan executed against a build
A test cycle and its executions, in Jira

prompt: A testing group serves three products whose teams use three different trackers, and each product needs a coverage report every week. Which kind of tool fits?
hint: Start from where the work already happens.

choices.text: Zephyr, installed in the Jira of whichever team asks first
choices.why: Two of the three products would have their cases in a tracker they do not use.

choices.text: One spreadsheet per product, merged by hand each week
choices.why: Three files merged weekly is the sign of having outgrown a spreadsheet.

choices.text: A standalone case manager such as TestRail or qTest
choices.why: Right: it sits beside every tracker instead of inside one of them.

choices.text: No case tool; the coverage report belongs in the trackers
choices.why: Three trackers give three partial reports and no single view.

prompt: In cases.csv, how many cases failed on release 1.1?
hint: Count the cells in the 1.1 column that start with failed.

prompt: Why does TC-17 have no result in the 1.0 column?
hint: When was it written?

choices.text: It passed on 1.0, and in this file a pass is left blank
choices.why: Passes are written as passed, as every other row shows.

choices.text: It was written after lesson 14 found the defect on 1.1
choices.why: Right: the case did not exist when 1.0 was run, and the blank says so.

choices.text: The Book page did not exist on 1.0
choices.why: It did; release 1.1 changed three lines and none of them added a page.

choices.text: Ana skipped it on 1.0 to save time before the release
choices.why: A skipped case still exists; this one had not been written.

prompt: The 1.1 cell of TC-13 reads failed: refunded. What does section 04 see wrong with a cell like that?
hint: How many things is it holding?

choices.text: Status and evidence in one string, with no link to a defect
choices.why: Right: a typo in the status breaks every count, and refunded is not a link to a report.

choices.text: It should say passed, because the refund itself worked as designed
choices.why: The refund working is the defect: a used order must not be refunded.

choices.text: It is too short to be evidence
choices.why: Its length is not the problem; mixing two things in one cell is.

choices.text: Results belong in a separate file per run, not in the case table
choices.why: A file per run loses the row that makes history visible.

prompt: Next month TC-13's steps are rewritten in the spreadsheet. What has happened to its 1.0 result?
hint: What text was 1.0 actually run against?

choices.text: Nothing; a result belongs to the release, not to the steps
choices.why: It belongs to the steps that were run, and those are gone.

choices.text: It becomes not run until 1.0 is tested again
choices.why: The spreadsheet changes no cell by itself; the old result stays, now misleading.

choices.text: It sits beside steps never run on 1.0
choices.why: Right: a tool would keep the version of the case each result was recorded against.

choices.text: It moves to the new steps automatically, as in every tool
choices.why: A spreadsheet keeps the latest text and nothing else.

prompt: When a spreadsheet needs written ___ about how to edit it, those are the features of a case tool, kept by hand.
hint: The rule of thumb at the end of section 04.

prompt: Which of these does a case tool keep, by section 01? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Four things, kept apart.

choices.text: A repository of cases grouped in suites
choices.why: Right: the cases, written once.

choices.text: Runs, each with one result per case
choices.why: Right: every execution against a build.

choices.text: Links from cases to requirements and from failures to defects
choices.why: Right: traceability, walked either way.

choices.text: The ranking of risks that decides which cases run first
choices.why: That is a decision in the plan of lesson 1; the tool records what it produces.

choices.text: The steps of each case, written from the requirement
choices.why: People write the steps; the tool stores them.

prompt: Ana filters cases.csv for R3 and gets no rows. What does that tell her?
hint: What is a filter on the requirement column?

choices.text: R3 passes, since no case has failed against it
choices.why: No case means nothing was checked, so nothing passed either.

choices.text: R3 was left out of scope
choices.why: Lesson 1's plan puts R2 to R9 in scope; this is a gap, not a decision.

choices.text: No case covers it: a coverage gap
choices.why: Right: an empty filter is the most useful thing a coverage view shows.

choices.text: The filter is broken
choices.why: It found nothing because there is nothing; R5 returns three rows the same way.

prompt: In a run of twenty cases, five that were blocked by one crash are marked failed. What does the run's failure count now tell the team?
hint: Which question does failed answer?

choices.text: That five behaviours are wrong, when nobody tested them
choices.why: Right: the count reports findings that were never made, and hides one defect behind five.

choices.text: The same as before, since blocked and failed are both bad
choices.why: They answer different questions: wrong, or untested.

choices.text: More than it would, which is safer for a release decision
choices.why: An inflated count sends people to fix five things that may be fine.

choices.text: Nothing, because counts are not read
choices.why: Lesson 19 builds a report on exactly these counts.

prompt: TC-10 passed on 1.0 and failed on 1.1. One case whose result went from pass to fail after a change is called a ___.
hint: Lesson 10's subject.
